1a.html:
Absolute poverty is the inability to meet basic needs, measured as income below a fixed real line (USD 1.90 a day at PPP). Growth is needed to end it, but growth alone does not guarantee it.

Why growth is necessary

  • In a poor country, redistributing a small income cannot lift everyone above the line.
  • Growth creates jobs, income and the tax revenue that pays for schools, health care and transfers.
  • China's fast growth cut its headcount ratio from 64% (1981) to 10% (2004).

Why it is not sufficient

  • The character of growth decides who gains. Under modern-sector enrichment growth (Fields), income rises only for those already in the modern sector: GNI grows, inequality rises and poverty is unchanged.
  • The poor lack land, credit, health and education, so capital-intensive or urban-biased growth bypasses them.
  • Growth itself need not change inequality: East Asia grew 5.5% a year per head and Africa shrank, yet both Gini coefficients barely moved.

Hence growth must be shared, through labour-intensive growth, asset redistribution, investment in the human capital of the poor, credit and safety nets.
pts: Defines absolute poverty (below a fixed real line, for example USD 1.90 a day; later revisions also credited) or relative inequality
Necessary: redistribution of a small income cannot end poverty; growth raises income and jobs
Necessary: growth funds public services and transfers, or evidence such as China's fall from 64% to 10%
Not sufficient: the character of growth decides who gains, for example modern-sector enrichment leaves poverty unchanged
The poor lack assets, credit and human capital, so growth can bypass them
Growth need not reduce inequality (unchanged Gini despite fast growth, or the Kuznets rise)
Policies needed alongside growth, for example asset redistribution, education and health, credit or safety nets
1a.src: Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 31, 36-40, 44, 55-56; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 276-284, 292-293, 298-299
1a.watch:
• "Necessary" and "not sufficient" are two separate arguments; give reasons for each, not just a list of policies.
  • Poverty can also fall without fast growth (traditional-sector enrichment, as in Sri Lanka and Kerala), but not far or for long.

1b.html:
Growth needs not only new machines and scientific knowledge but also new rules, organisations and social arrangements that let people use them productively. Institutions are the "rules of the game" (North): property rights, contract enforcement, the rule of law, checks on elites, and informal norms.

Why they matter as much

  1. Technology must be financed, adopted and spread. Inventions raise output only where incentives, credit and markets exist; the limited-liability company, banks and patent law made industrial technology pay.
  2. Institutions explain income gaps. Technology is available worldwide, yet countries diverge: North and South Korea; former colonies given extractive institutions stayed poorer than those with secure property rights (Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson).
  3. Social innovations raise output with little new technology. Land reform in South Korea and Taiwan and China's household responsibility system (1978) raised farm output; in Bangladesh, Grameen's group lending gave credit without collateral.
  4. Capital alone is not sufficient. The Marshall Plan worked because Europe had the institutions to use new capital (slide 20).

Conclusion: the two are complements: technology sets what is possible; institutions decide whether it is used.
pts: Interprets the statement: growth needs new rules, organisations and social arrangements, not only inventions
Defines institutions as the rules of the game (property rights, contracts, rule of law, norms)
Explains that technology needs institutions to be financed, adopted and diffused, with an example
Shows that institutions explain divergence despite shared technology (Korea, colonial institutions or similar)
Gives a social or institutional innovation that raised output (microcredit, land reform, household responsibility system, mobile money or similar)
Concludes that they are complements, or that capital and technology are necessary but not sufficient
1b.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 20-21, 27, 35; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 115-117, 124, 133
1b.watch:
• This is Todaro's chapter 2 discussion question 7; the chapter 3 slides touch it only through the "necessary but not sufficient" critique and the Lewis model's neglect of institutions.
  • Do not argue that technology does not matter; the statement says institutions are "as important", not more important.
  • Any well-explained example of an institutional or social innovation earns the example marks.

2a.fix: • hum-ch2 slides 14 and 20 say the education index uses a geometric mean and the maxima are the observed maxima. That was the 2010 to 2013 method. Since the 2014 Report the goalposts are fixed (85 yr, 18 yr, 15 yr, USD 75,000) and the education index is the arithmetic mean of the two schooling indices (hum-hdr p 2).
2a.html:
The Human Development Index (HDI) is UNDP's composite index, from 0 to 1, of a country's average achievement in a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living. It is computed in two steps.

Step 1: dimension indices. Each indicator is scaled between fixed goalposts:

I = \frac{\text{actual value} - \text{minimum}}{\text{maximum} - \text{minimum}}
  • Health: life expectancy at birth, goalposts 20 and 85 years.
  • Education: expected years of schooling (0 to 18) and mean years of schooling (0 to 15); the education index I_E is the arithmetic mean of the two.
  • Income: GNI per capita at 2011 purchasing power parity (PPP: rates that equalise the cost of a common basket), USD 100 to 75,000, in natural logs (diminishing marginal utility): I_I = (\ln \mathrm{GNI} - \ln 100)/(\ln 75000 - \ln 100).

Step 2: geometric mean of the three indices.

\mathrm{HDI} = \left(I_H \times I_E \times I_I\right)^{1/3}

The dimensions are imperfect substitutes, so poor performance in any one pulls the HDI down; the old HDI's arithmetic mean let one dimension compensate fully for another.

Example (Bangladesh, HDR 2019): I_H = (72.3-20)/65 = 0.805, I_E = (11.2/18 + 6.1/15)/2 = 0.514, I_I = \ln(4057/100)/\ln 750 = 0.559, so \mathrm{HDI} = (0.805 \times 0.514 \times 0.559)^{1/3} = 0.614.

Classes: very high 0.800 and above, high 0.700 to 0.799, medium 0.550 to 0.699, low below 0.550; Bangladesh is medium.
pts: Defines the HDI: a composite 0 to 1 index of health, knowledge and living standard
Names the four indicators: life expectancy at birth, expected and mean years of schooling, GNI per capita at PPP
Dimension index = (actual - minimum)/(maximum - minimum), with goalposts 20 to 85 yr, 0 to 18, 0 to 15 and USD 100 to 75,000 (the slides' observed maxima also accepted)
Education index as the mean of the two schooling indices (arithmetic, or the slides' geometric version)
Income index in natural logs because of diminishing marginal utility of income
\mathrm{HDI} = (I_H I_E I_I)^{1/3}, the geometric mean of the three indices
Geometric mean: imperfect substitutability, so a weak dimension pulls the HDI down
Works an example through to the HDI, for example Bangladesh 0.614 or the slides' Ghana 0.558
States the classes with cut-offs 0.800, 0.700 and 0.550
2a.src: Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 13-20; HDR 2019 technical notes, pp 2-3; Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 15-19; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 89-90, 144
2a.watch:
• The Ghana example (hum-ch2 slide 19) uses the 2010 to 2013 version: observed maxima of 83.6 yr, 13.3 yr and USD 87,478, and a geometric-mean education index divided by 0.971 (HDI 0.558). Either version earns credit if the goalposts are stated; do not mix them.
  • Only income is logged. An index cannot exceed 1: income above USD 75,000 is capped.
  • 0.614 is the 2018 value. The latest value on hum-dim slide 20 is 0.670 (rank 129 of 193), still medium.
  • The traditional HDI (1990 to 2009) was the arithmetic mean of life expectancy (25 to 85 yr), education (2/3 adult literacy + 1/3 gross enrolment) and log GDP per capita (USD 100 to 40,000); Bangladesh 2007 gave 0.543 (hum-todaro p 144).

2b.html:
The HDI combines life expectancy, schooling and log GNI per capita into one 0 to 1 index. Beyond the usual points (broader than income; arbitrary weights):

Additional strengths

  • Outcomes, not inputs. It measures how long people live and how much schooling they get, not how much is spent, so wasteful spending earns no credit.
  • Accountability. Published ranks push governments to compete on health and education; the slides, for example, compare Bangladesh's rank (129) with India (134) and Pakistan (164).

Additional weaknesses

  • Saturation at the top. Life expectancy and schooling have ceilings, so rich countries cluster near 1 and the HDI separates them poorly.
  • No sustainability. The HDI can rise while forests, groundwater or the climate are run down.
  • Data problems. Missing indicators are estimated by regression, and the values lag by a year or two.

What I would do differently

  • Adjust each dimension for inequality, because averages hide who gains.
  • Add an environmental or freedom dimension, because development should expand lasting freedoms, not only incomes.
  • Use learning-adjusted schooling, because years in school are not skills.
pts: An additional strength with its reason, for example it measures outcomes, not spending
A second strength, for example ranks create accountability or the index can be split by region or group
An additional weakness, for example saturation near 1 among rich countries
A second weakness, for example no sustainability or environmental cost, or GNI's flaws
A third weakness, for example imputed or lagged data, or expected schooling as a forecast
A first design change with its reason, for example an inequality adjustment
A second design change with its reason, for example an environment or freedom dimension, or quality-adjusted schooling (any sound change with a reason earns the credit)
2b.src: Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 13-21; Dimensions of economic development (v3), slide 20; HDR 2019 technical notes, p 2; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 92-94, 145
2b.watch:
• "Additional" comes from the textbook question: points beyond the standard list earn the most, but the standard ones (broader than income, arbitrary weights, hidden inequality, quantity not quality) still earn credit if explained.
  • UNDP's own fixes exist: the inequality-adjusted HDI, the Gender Inequality Index and, since 2020, a planetary-pressures-adjusted HDI.
  • Keep each point to one reason; a list of labels earns little in an "explain" answer.

3a.html:
Per capita income is a country's gross national income divided by its population: the average income per person, in USD at exchange rates or purchasing power parity (PPP).

Level of living is the actual condition in which people live: food, shelter and clothing, health, education, security and freedom. Low levels of living show up as absolute poverty, malnutrition, short life expectancy, illiteracy and poor housing.

Distinctions

AspectLow per capita incomeLow levels of living
Naturea monetary average, a meansactual well-being, the end
MeasureGNI per capita (PPP)life expectancy, infant mortality, literacy, nutrition; HDI, MPI
Distributionsilent: an average hides who gets whatwhat most people actually have
Depends onoutput and productivityincome plus public services, gender, governance, non-market goods
Remedygrowthgrowth with public provision and redistribution

Link. The two are correlated, since income is the main means to a good life, but they differ: Bangladesh, at a GNI per capita of USD 3,677 (PPP), had a higher HDI (0.608) than Pakistan at USD 5,311 (0.562). Low income is one cause of low levels of living, not the same thing.
pts: Defines per capita income: GNI divided by population, an average in money terms (exchange rate or PPP)
Defines levels of living: actual conditions of food, shelter, health, education, security and freedom
Distinction: an income average (means) against actual well-being (end)
Distinction: measured by GNI per capita against social indicators such as life expectancy, literacy, HDI or MPI
Distinction: per capita income ignores distribution; levels of living reflect what most people have
Distinction: levels of living also depend on public services, gender, governance or non-market goods
Example showing the gap (Bangladesh against Pakistan, Cuba, or similar)
Concludes that the two are related but not the same
3a.src: Ch 1 Economic development (Todaro), slides 7-14, 16-23; Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 2, 13, 21-25; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 11-13
3a.watch:
• "Show the distinctions" suits a table; define both terms first.
  • Todaro's list of common characteristics of developing countries opens with "lower levels of living and productivity"; low income is only one part of that.
  • The HDI figures are from the 2018 Human Development Report table on the slides; quote them as approximate.

3b.html:
Yes. Per capita income is an average and a means; levels of living are what people actually achieve, and a high average can coexist with poor health, schooling and housing ("growth without development").

How it happens

  1. Unequal distribution: income concentrated in a small elite leaves the majority poor despite a high average.
  2. Resource enclaves: oil or mineral exports raise GNI with few jobs or links, and elites capture the rents.
  3. Weak public provision: little spent on health, schooling and water.
  4. Discrimination and governance: women, minorities or migrants are excluded; corruption diverts resources.

Examples (2018 HDR, GNI per capita at PPP)

  • Equatorial Guinea: about USD 19,500, yet HDI 0.591 and life expectancy 57.9 years; its HDI rank is 80 places below its income rank.
  • Gabon: USD 16,431, HDI 0.702, 40 places lower on HDI than on income.
  • South Africa: USD 11,923 but HDI 0.699 and life expectancy 63.4, from extreme inequality and HIV.
  • By contrast Cuba (USD 7,524, HDI 0.777) and Sri Lanka do far better than their incomes suggest.

Conclusion: high income is necessary but not sufficient; what matters is how it is distributed and converted into capabilities.
pts: Answers yes, explaining that per capita income is an average and a means while levels of living are actual achievements
Mechanism: unequal distribution of income leaves the majority poor
Mechanism: resource enclave whose rents are captured by elites, with few jobs or links
Mechanism: weak public provision, discrimination or poor governance
At least two real examples with figures (Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Botswana, South Africa or Gulf states)
Contrast case (Cuba or Sri Lanka) or conclusion that income is necessary but not sufficient
3b.src: Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 21-23; Ch 1 Economic development (Todaro), slides 18-21; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 13, 25-27
3b.watch:
• "Explain with examples" needs real countries with numbers; a purely hypothetical answer loses most of the example marks.
  • The table's "GNI per capita rank minus HDI rank" column is the quickest evidence: large negative values (Equatorial Guinea -80, Gabon -40) mark low levels of living for the income.
  • Older textbooks cite Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and other Gulf states for the same point; they are acceptable examples.

4.html:
The Lewis two-sector model (W. Arthur Lewis, 1954) is a theory of development in which surplus labour from traditional agriculture moves to a modern industrial sector, whose growth absorbs it and industrialises the economy.

Assumptions

  • Traditional sector: overpopulated subsistence farming with surplus labour: the marginal product of labour, MP_{LA}, is zero, so workers can leave without loss of output. Output is shared, so the rural income W_A equals the average product.
  • Modern sector: employers hire until MP_{LM} equals the wage, so the MP_{LM} curve is the labour demand curve.
  • The urban wage W_M is fixed at a premium over W_A, and at that wage labour supply is unlimited (a horizontal curve).

Mechanism. With capital K_{M1}, employment is L_1 where D_1 meets W_M (point F). Output 0D_1FL_1 is split into wages 0W_MFL_1 and profits W_MD_1F. Capitalists reinvest all profits, so capital rises, demand shifts to D_2 and D_3, and employment grows to L_2 and L_3 at a constant wage. This continues until the surplus is absorbed (the Lewis turning point); then wages rise. The result is structural transformation from agriculture to industry.

Criticisms

  1. Jobs need not grow with capital. If profits buy labour-saving machines, the new demand curve is steeper and crosses the old one at the wage: output and profits rise, but employment stays at L_1. Profits may also leave the country as capital flight.
  2. No rural surplus, no urban full employment. Research finds little surplus labour in most rural areas (except seasonally), while cities have large open unemployment.
  3. Urban wages are not constant. Unions, civil-service pay scales and multinationals' practices pushed urban wages up even with unemployment; institutional factors play little part in the model.
  4. Diminishing returns in industry are assumed, but some industries show increasing returns.
  5. Agriculture and human capital are neglected. Without rising farm productivity, food prices rise and squeeze industrial profits; skills and health are ignored.

Conclusion: a valuable early picture of structural change that fits Western history and China (turning point about 2010), but its assumptions need major changes for most developing countries today.
pts: Defines the model: surplus labour moves from traditional agriculture to a growing modern industrial sector
Surplus labour with MP_{LA} = 0; rural income equals the average product
Fixed urban wage above rural income with an unlimited (horizontal) labour supply
Employment where MP_{LM} equals the wage, with output split into wages and profits (in words or on a diagram)
All profits reinvested: capital rises, demand shifts out, employment grows at a constant wage
Lewis turning point and structural transformation as the outcome
Criticism: labour-saving reinvestment (or capital flight) raises output without raising employment
Criticism: little rural surplus labour, while urban unemployment exists
Criticism: urban wages rise through institutional forces (unions, pay scales, multinationals); institutions ignored
Criticism: increasing, not diminishing, returns in some industries
Criticism: neglect of agriculture's productivity or of human capital, or another sound criticism
Balanced conclusion: useful for China and the West, needs modification elsewhere
4.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 22-28; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 163-168
4.watch:
• "Discuss with criticisms" wants both halves: about half the marks for the model and half for the criticisms.
  • The slides list four criticisms (labour transfer not proportional to capital accumulation, rural surplus and urban full employment, diminishing returns, institutions); Todaro adds human capital. Agriculture's role is the Fei-Ranis extension.
  • Criticism 1 is best shown by the crossing demand curves of the second figure; describing it in words earns the same marks.

5a.html:
Private foreign investment is investment by foreign private firms and investors: mainly foreign direct investment (FDI), in which a multinational corporation (MNC) owns and controls a business in the host country, and portfolio investment in shares and bonds.

Arguments for: it fills gaps

  1. Saving gap: a 7% growth target with capital-output ratio 3 needs 21% saving (s = cg); if only 16% is saved, FDI fills the 5% gap.
  2. Foreign-exchange gap: capital inflow, later export earnings.
  3. Revenue gap: taxes on MNC profits.
  4. Skills and technology gap: management, know-how and market contacts, as Daewoo's training of Desh Garments' workers seeded Bangladesh's RMG industry.

Arguments against: it may widen gaps

  1. Crowding out of local saving, firms and credit.
  2. Balance-of-payments drain from imported inputs and repatriated profits, royalties and fees.
  3. Transfer pricing and tax concessions shrink the tax gain.
  4. Capital-intensive technology: few jobs, suppressed local entrepreneurship.
  5. Dualism and inequality, elite consumption.
  6. Political power (a "race to the bottom" for concessions); portfolio flows are volatile "hot money".

Conclusion: the evidence is mixed; benefits depend on the terms and on the host government's bargaining power.
pts: Defines private foreign investment: FDI by MNCs (ownership and control) and portfolio investment
For: fills the saving gap (with the s = cg logic) and the foreign-exchange gap
For: fills the tax-revenue gap and the management, technology and skills gap
For: jobs, exports or skill spillovers (the Desh-Daewoo example is optional)
Against: may lower domestic saving or crowd out local investment
Against: balance-of-payments drain from imports and repatriation, and lost tax through transfer pricing
Against: inappropriate technology, few jobs, suppressed local entrepreneurship, dualism or inequality
Against: political influence, race to the bottom or volatile portfolio flows
Concludes that the outcome depends on terms and bargaining power
5a.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 795-803
5a.watch:
• "Summarize" asks for both sides in brief; a one-sided answer loses half the marks.
  • Todaro organises the case around the four gaps; matching each "for" with its "against" (saving, foreign exchange, tax, skills) is the clearest structure.
  • Todaro's evidence point: both MNCs and portfolio investors tend to follow growth rather than lead it.

5b.html:
The aim is to raise the host country's share of the benefits (jobs, skills, technology, exports, tax) while keeping the investment profitable and predictable for the investor.

  1. Target and screen. An investment promotion agency (in Bangladesh, the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority and the Bangladesh Economic Zones Authority) steers FDI towards export-oriented, labour-intensive and technology-bringing sectors.
  2. Moderate performance requirements: local staff training, export targets, phased local sourcing, agreed in advance and within WTO rules.
  3. Local participation: joint ventures and gradual local equity, not forced majority ownership (the Andean Pact's fade-out rules of the 1970s deterred investors).
  4. Fair taxation: short tax holidays, arm's-length rules against transfer pricing, regional coordination against underbidding.
  5. Linkage programmes: supplier development so MNCs buy locally, where spillovers occur.
  6. Labour, safety and environmental standards, backed by buyers' social-responsibility schemes (the Accord after Rana Plaza).
  7. Favour long-term FDI over short-term "hot money".
  8. Keep the incentives: stable policy, rule of law, infrastructure, a one-stop service, guaranteed profit repatriation.

Conclusion: clear, stable rules that share the gains work better than heavy controls; a large market or coordinated bargaining raises the host's leverage, as China's experience shows.
pts: Targets and screens FDI to priority sectors through an investment promotion agency or economic zones
Performance requirements (training, exports, local sourcing), moderate and agreed in advance
Joint ventures or gradual local ownership, without forcing investors out
Fair taxation: limited tax holidays, rules against transfer pricing, or coordination against a race to the bottom
Linkage and supplier-development programmes for spillovers
Labour, safety and environmental standards or corporate social responsibility
Preference for long-term FDI over short-term portfolio flows
Keeps investor incentives: stability, rule of law, infrastructure, one-stop service, profit repatriation
Concludes that stable, gain-sharing rules beat heavy controls; bargaining power matters
5b.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 799-803; Standard textbook treatment
5b.watch:
• The question's condition "without destroying all incentives" must be answered: each control needs its matching assurance to the investor.
  • Todaro's list (stricter regulation, tougher bargaining, shopping around, performance standards, more domestic ownership, coordination among host countries) is the core; the Bangladesh agencies are examples.
  • Any sound strategy with a reason earns the same credit.

6a.html:
Project evaluation assesses whether a project is worth its resources, before, during and after implementation.

Stages (project cycle)

  1. Identification: screen ideas against plan priorities.
  2. Preparation: feasibility study of technical, market, financial and environmental aspects of the alternatives.
  3. Appraisal: financial analysis at market prices, then economic analysis at shadow prices (transfers out, externalities in), then social analysis of who gains.
  4. Implementation and monitoring: mid-term evaluation of cost, time and targets.
  5. Ex-post evaluation: results compared with forecasts; lessons fed back.

Methods of evaluation

  • Discounted: NPV = \sum (B_t - C_t)/(1+r)^t, accept if above 0; BCR = PV(B)/PV(C), accept if above 1; IRR, the rate giving NPV = 0, accept if above r.
  • Undiscounted: payback period (years to recover the investment) and accounting rate of return.

NPV is the primary method; the others support it.
pts: Defines project evaluation (worth of a project before, during and after)
Identification and preparation or feasibility study
Appraisal: financial, economic (shadow prices) and social analysis
Implementation monitoring and ex-post evaluation with feedback
Discounted methods: NPV > 0, BCR > 1, IRR above the discount rate, each with its formula or definition
Undiscounted methods: payback (or accounting rate of return)
States that NPV is the primary method
6a.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 607-610; CBA exam note, pp 5-9; Solved problems: NPV, IRR, payback, p 4; Cost-benefit analysis handout, handout parts VIII and XII; Standard textbook treatment
6a.watch:
• Two tasks in 8 marks: keep each stage to a line.
  • A student who explains the appraisal stages (Todaro's objectives, shadow prices with a social discount rate, decision criterion) instead of the project cycle should earn the stage marks.

6b.html:
Definitions (end-of-year flows, year 0 = now, discount rate r):

  • NPV is the present value of benefits minus that of costs, \mathrm{NPV} = \sum_{t=0}^{n} (B_t - C_t)/(1+r)^t. Accept if positive; NPV = 0 means the project earns exactly r.
  • BCR is benefit per taka of cost, \mathrm{BCR} = PV(B)/PV(C). Accept if above 1 (the same test as NPV > 0).
  • IRR is the discount rate at which NPV = 0. Accept if it exceeds the social discount rate.

For example, Tk 100,000 now returning Tk 40,000, 50,000 and 60,000 in years 1 to 3 gives, at 10%, NPV = Tk 22,765, BCR = 1.23 and IRR = 21.6%.

Interpretation. Given: NPV = Tk 472,851.99 lakh, BCR = 1.398, IRR = 33.55%.

  • NPV is positive: discounted benefits exceed discounted costs by Tk 472,851.99 lakh (about Tk 4,729 crore) at the chosen discount rate, so the project adds net value to society: accept.
  • BCR is 1.398: each Tk 1 of present-value cost returns Tk 1.40 of benefit. Benefits could fall about 28% (1 - 1/1.398), or costs rise about 40%, before BCR reaches 1.
  • IRR is 33.55%: the resources earn 33.55% a year, far above the social discount rates commonly used (roughly 8 to 12%). NPV stays positive at any rate below 33.55%.
  • Implied size: PV(C) = \mathrm{NPV}/(\mathrm{BCR} - 1) = 472{,}851.99/0.398 = 1{,}188{,}070 lakh Tk and PV(B) = 1.398 \times PV(C) = 1{,}660{,}922 lakh Tk.

Answer: all three criteria agree: the project is economically viable and should be approved, subject to sensitivity analysis.
pts: NPV defined as PV(B) - PV(C) with the formula; accept if positive
BCR defined as PV(B)/PV(C); accept if above 1
IRR defined as the discount rate giving NPV = 0; accept if above the social discount rate
NPV: discounted benefits exceed discounted costs by Tk 472,851.99 lakh (about Tk 4,729 crore); accept
BCR 1.398: Tk 1.40 of benefit per Tk 1 of cost; benefits may fall about 28% or costs rise about 40% before BCR = 1
IRR 33.55% far above the social discount rate; NPV positive at any rate below it
Implied PV of costs (about Tk 1,188,070 lakh) and benefits (about Tk 1,660,922 lakh)
Concludes that all three agree and the project should be approved
6b.src: CBA exam note, pp 5-9; Solved problems: NPV, IRR, payback, pp 1-2; Cost-benefit analysis handout, handout parts IV, V, VII and X; Standard textbook treatment
6b.watch:
• Lakh taka is the unit: Tk 472,851.99 lakh is Tk 4,728.5 crore.
  • The implied PVs assume the gross BCR at the same discount rate as the NPV.
  • Of the four papers with this question, this project has the smallest NPV and BCR but still passes comfortably.

7a.html:
Theory of balanced growth

Balanced growth (Nurkse, 1953; Rosenstein-Rodan) is a strategy of simultaneous investment in a wide range of complementary industries, and in agriculture and industry together.

  • Reason: the small market limits the inducement to invest. A lone shoe factory fails because poor workers cannot buy shoes; if many industries start together, their workers become each other's customers, breaking the vicious circle of poverty on the demand side.
  • Criticism: it needs capital, skills and administrative capacity a poor country lacks, and ignores exports.

Theory of unbalanced growth

Unbalanced growth (Hirschman, 1958) is a strategy of deliberate investment in a few key sectors with the strongest linkages: backward (they raise demand for inputs) and forward (they supply cheap inputs to users).

  • Mechanism: the resulting shortages and surpluses send profit signals that induce investment in lagging sectors: a "chain of disequilibria" that economises on scarce decision-making ability.
  • Two paths: excess social overhead capital (SOC: power and roads first, inviting directly productive activities, DPA) or a shortage of SOC (factories first, whose bottlenecks press for infrastructure).
  • Criticism: bottlenecks, inflation, regional inequality. Example: Bangladesh's garment-led growth with its spinning and dyeing linkages.
pts: Balanced growth defined: simultaneous investment in many complementary sectors (Nurkse, Rosenstein-Rodan)
Its reason: small market limits the inducement to invest; sectors create demand for each other
Breaks the vicious circle of poverty, or a criticism (resource requirement, neglect of trade)
Unbalanced growth defined: investment in key sectors with strongest backward and forward linkages (Hirschman)
Its mechanism: imbalances create signals and pressures that induce further investment (chain of disequilibria)
The SOC and DPA paths (excess or shortage of social overhead capital)
A criticism of unbalanced growth or an example (Bangladesh RMG linkages)
7a.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 215-216, 225, 687; Standard textbook treatment
7a.watch:
• "Explain in short": the definition plus the reasoning for each theory is the core; the SOC and DPA paths are what lift an answer to full marks.
  • No course slides cover these theories; they follow standard development texts, with linkages as in Todaro chapter 4.
  • Do not present them only as opposites: both aim at the same goal, overcoming the small-market trap, and differ on how fast and how widely to invest.

7b.html:
Industrialisation is the rise of manufacturing in output, exports and jobs. SDG 9 calls for "inclusive and sustainable industrialisation", and industry also bears on SDGs 1, 5, 8 and 12. Bangladesh's industry is narrow: RMG is 84% of exports and private investment is stuck near 23% of GDP.

Recommended policies (with the SDGs they serve)

  1. Export diversification: incentives for leather, light engineering, pharmaceuticals, agro-processing and ICT (SDGs 8, 9).
  2. Economic zones and infrastructure: complete the planned economic zones with reliable power, gas, ports and roads (SDGs 7, 9).
  3. Investment climate and finance: policy stability, FDI promotion and credit for SMEs (SDGs 8, 9.3).
  4. Skills and technology: TVET linked to industry, R&D, digital and 4IR skills (SDGs 4, 9.5).
  5. Green industry: effluent treatment, energy efficiency, renewable power and a circular economy in textiles (SDGs 6, 12, 13).
  6. Decent work: safe workplaces, enforced minimum wages and childcare so women can work (SDGs 5, 8).
  7. Trade strategy for LDC graduation: negotiate trade agreements and GSP+ to keep market access (SDG 17).
  8. Regional balance: rural and agro-based industries in lagging districts (SDGs 1, 10).

Conclusion: a diversified, green, labour-intensive industrial strategy serves SDG 9 and most other goals.

• "Recommend" asks for your policies: give each with a reason and the SDG it serves; any sound policy of this kind earns its point.

8a.html:
Developing countries should seek aid that adds more to development than it costs, on the following terms and conditions.

Terms

  1. Highly concessional: grants, or loans with a grant element of at least about 35% (the IMF and World Bank threshold): low interest, maturity of 30 years or more and a long grace period.
  2. Untied: freedom to buy from the cheapest supplier through open tender.
  3. Aligned and predictable: multi-year, on-budget and in support of the country's own plan (the 2005 Paris Declaration principles: ownership, alignment, harmonisation, results, mutual accountability).
  4. Few conditions: only those the country would choose anyway; no political or military strings.

Conditions for accepting

  1. Returns above cost: the funded project should show a positive net present value at the social discount rate after counting repayment, and fit national priorities (infrastructure gaps, health, education, climate adaptation).
  2. Repayment capacity: loans only for projects that earn or save foreign exchange, keeping debt service within sustainable limits.
  3. Absorptive capacity: local staff, counterpart funds and maintenance budgets exist; technical assistance must train local people.
  4. Transparency: open procurement, audit and monitoring against corruption.

Conclusion: aid should complement domestic saving and trade, not replace them.
pts: Concessional terms: grants or soft loans (high grant element, low interest, long maturity and grace)
Untied aid with open, competitive procurement
Aid aligned with national plans, predictable and country-owned (Paris Declaration principles)
Limited conditions, no political strings
Accept only for priority projects whose returns exceed the full cost of the aid
Loans only where repayment capacity exists: foreign-exchange earning projects, sustainable debt service
Absorptive capacity and training of local staff through technical assistance
Transparency and anti-corruption safeguards
Concludes that aid should complement, not replace, domestic effort

8a.watch:
• "Do you think" invites your view: any sound condition with a reason earns credit.
  • The 35% grant-element threshold is the IMF and World Bank concessionality test (with a 5% discount rate); the older OECD definition of aid used 25%. Either earns credit if stated as a threshold.
  • No course slides cover aid; this follows Todaro chapter 14 (concessional terms, tying, absorptive capacity, the Paris Declaration).

8b.html:
My view: no, not whatever they can get. Each offer should be judged on its net benefit and accepted only if it pays.

The case for accepting less-than-ideal aid

  • A binding saving or foreign-exchange gap (two-gap model) holds growth down; some finance beats none when poverty is urgent.
  • Humanitarian aid (floods, cyclones, refugees) should be taken whatever its form.
  • Aid-financed infrastructure can unlock private investment and help escape a poverty trap.

The case against accepting everything

  • Tied, hard loans can cost more than they give: overpricing, interest and exchange-rate risk may leave a negative grant element.
  • Debt traps: Sri Lanka's Hambantota port, leased to a Chinese firm in 2017, preceded its 2022 default.
  • Dependency, lost policy freedom, weaker tax effort, "white elephant" projects.

A decision rule: accept an offer only if the present value of its benefits exceeds the present value of all costs, including the tying premium and debt service in foreign exchange; otherwise negotiate or shop among donors.

Alternatives: domestic revenue (Bangladesh's tax-to-GDP ratio is below 8%), exports, FDI, remittances; Bangladesh self-financed the Padma Bridge after the World Bank withdrew in 2012.

Conclusion: accept aid selectively; bad aid can be worse than no aid.
pts: States a clear, reasoned stance (selective acceptance; a reasoned "yes" or "no" also earns this)
The case for accepting: binding saving or foreign-exchange gaps, urgent poverty, humanitarian aid, or the poverty-trap argument
The cost of bad aid: tying premium, interest and exchange-rate risk, or a debt-trap example (Sri Lanka or another)
Dependency, loss of sovereignty, weaker tax effort or white-elephant projects
A decision rule: accept only if the PV of benefits exceeds the full PV of costs
Alternatives: domestic revenue, exports, FDI, remittances or other finance (the Padma Bridge example is optional)
Concludes that aid should be accepted selectively
8b.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 810-815; Bangladesh and the SDGs (2026), slide 12; Standard textbook treatment
8b.watch:
• This is a "discuss your view" question: a sound case for accepting imperfect aid (two-gap model, emergencies) earns full credit if it is argued and weighed against the costs.
  • The Hambantota example is contested: most of Sri Lanka's debt was market borrowing, not Chinese loans; use it as an illustration of costly project debt, not as the single cause of the default.
  • The tax-to-GDP figure is from hum-sdg slide 12.
